title: Ladders & Stepladders
whatItIs: Ladders aren't banned, but they don't prevent or mitigate a fall. Use one only when a risk assessment shows better equipment isn't justified because the risk is low and the job short.

keyFacts.text: Ladder use MUST be justified by a risk assessment: low risk, and short use or site features you can't alter.
A secure handhold and secure support MUST always be available to the person on the ladder.
A portable ladder MUST be stopped from slipping: secure the stiles or use a stability device.

keyFacts: Use the 1-in-4 rule: one unit out for every four units up (a 75° angle).
Maintain three points of contact when climbing and wherever possible at the work position.
As a guide, if you'd be up a ladder for more than 30 minutes at a time, use other equipment.

visual.caption: Leaning ladder rules (HSE: Safe use of ladders and stepladders)

items.title: 1 in 4
items.text: One unit out at the base for every four units up: a 75° angle.

items.title: Not the top three rungs
items.text: Don't work off them. Extend at least 1 m or three rungs above where you work.

items.title: 1 m above the landing
items.text: A ladder used for access to another level: tied, and at least 1 m above the landing point.

items.title: 6 m from power lines
items.text: Not within 6 m horizontally of an overhead line unless it's dead or insulated.

a.label: Leaning ladder
points: Don't work off the top three rungs
Secure it: tie both stiles; footing is the last resort

b.label: Stepladder
points: Not the top three steps unless there's a suitable handhold
Face the work; avoid side-on loads such as side drilling

onTheTest.question: You are putting up a leaning ladder. What angle does HSE guidance recommend?
options: 1 unit out for every 4 units up
1 unit out for every 2 units up
1 unit out for every 1 unit up
Flat against the wall with no gap
onTheTest.why: HSE ladder guidance: use the 1-in-4 rule, one space or unit of measurement out for every four up, which is a 75° angle.

onTheTest.question: Which way of stopping a leaning ladder from slipping is the LAST resort?
options: Tying both stiles to a suitable point
Wedging the stiles against a wall
onTheTest.why: HSE: tie both stiles; if that isn't practical use a stability device; if not, securely wedge it. Footing is the last resort.

traps: Footing a ladder is the last resort, not the normal way to secure it.
Never stand a ladder on pallets, bricks, vans, towers or MEWPs: use firm, level ground.
Don't overreach: keep your belt buckle (or navel) within the stiles.
Found a defect in your pre-use check? Don't use the ladder: tell the person in charge.
